_source.displaydescription:
This non-existing rest house was constructed by a person named Dharaṇīdhara in 1694 CE (NS 814). Only a small shrine of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa remains at the center of the square pavilion where the Phalcā once stood.

The statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa faces west towards Umāmaheśvara Mandira (KIR0006) while the inscription recording the construction of the Phalcā is set on the rear wall of the shrine. The inscription states that Dharaṇīdhara, who constructed the Phalcā in 1694 CE, was a resident of Kirtipur and held the post of the chief of the fort. The fort probably is a reference to the city of Kirtipur. It further mentions that the Phalcā’s architecture was similar to Kaṣṭhamaṇḍapa of Kathmandu. The donor also endowed seven ropanīs of land to form a guthi for performing various rituals throughout the year (Shokoohy and others 2014, p. 94). The Phalcā is due to be reconstructed in traditional architecture with funds from the US embassy.

The statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa exudes the emotion of love, as the four-armed Nārāyaṇa is seen in amorous disposition, embracing his consort Lakṣmī while slightly bending towards her. Locals, therefore, call the deity ‘Khyālidyaḥ’, the deity of love. There is a local belief that worshipping Khyālidyaḥ brings the person’s love affair to a successful conclusion.

The inscription also instructs concerned persons to organize the hāthu hāyke tradition. This proves that the tradition of discharging fermented beer (thvã) from the Bhairava mask (Hāthudyaḥ) existed here. This tradition is no longer in practice.
_source.displayname: Kvāḥcva Khyālidyaḥ Phalcā || क्वाःच्व ख्यालिद्यः फल्चा ॥ KIR4066

_source.displaydescription:
Bhailaḥsĩ Bāhāḥ, a branch of Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440), can be reached via a narrow alley at the north-east corner of Bu Bāhāḥ and by passing through two small courtyards. This four-storey bāhāḥ stands in the north-west corner of its courtyard (10 m x 12 m).

A statue of Akṣobhya facing east is enshrined in the main sanctum, which is located on the ground floor and can be reached by climbing the stairs of a three bayed phalcā with a front row of columns. The central bay of this structure is surmounted by a carved toraṇa showing images of Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara. A painting of Buddhist images can be found on the mud plaster wall of the bāhāḥ's first floor. This level is also decorated with a lattice window flanked by two oval Tibetan-style paintings of Buddha‘s birth. A three-bayed window covers the principal façade on the third floor. An fourth floor has been added above the original floors, and now houses the āgama deity of the bāhāḥ. A private house to the north of the bāhāḥ exhiits similar Tibetan-style images of Caturmahārāja painted on oval mud plaster.

A dharmadhātu maṇḍala (85 cm high) is located in front of the bāhāḥ and a śikharakūṭa caitya (165 cm high) can be found at the center of the courtyard. There are three exits at the east, north-east, and south-east corners.

This bāhāḥ was established in 1896 (NS 1016) and is named after its founder, Bhairavasiṃha Vajrācārya.

_source.displaydescription:
Bhaiṣajyarāja Bāhāḥ, a branch of the Cikã Bahī (Saptapura Mahāvihāra, LAL1620), is located behind a five-bayed phalcā at the junction of the street from Bhelāchẽ and Bhindyaḥ Sataḥ at Cyāsal. The entrance to this Bāhāḥ is on a boundary wall to the west and it is attached to a phalcā to its south. The main structure is divided into three small rooms, consisting of a central sanctum room and two small rooms on either side. A small staircase in the eastern room leads up to the upper floor. The building shares a small space with a single-storey annex structure to its north.

The courtyard measures 7 m × 4.7 m, and has a residential building to the its east and north. Both of these are built on arcaded phalcās that serve as the ground floor. A caitya sits to the north of the Bāhāḥ, directly in front of its main door. The courtyard is paved with telia tiles. Small images of different Buddhist deities have been placed on the walls of the southern annex building and western boundary wall.

Jīvanṛsiṃha, a member of the Cikã Bahī and an Āyurvedic doctor (vaidya) by profession, established this Bāhāḥ in 1878 (NS 998). It takes its name from Jīvanṛsiṃha's profession; hence, it is known as Bhaiṣajyarāja Bāhāḥ. Wall paintings of the Five Buddhas can be found above the plain outer entrance, which is flanked by paintings of auspicious symbols. The north-facing god house has two storeys and a tiled roof supported by plain struts. Instead of a pinnacle, a small chimney (bhaipvāḥ) can be found on its sloping roof, as well as three metal banners displaying images of deities. The first floor of the god house is very low.

There is no toraṇa above the carved door of the sanctum, though it is flanked by two stone lions as it is customary. The lions also sit next to two metal flags that were donated in 1909 (NS 1023). The main facade of the god-house was decorated with wall paintings of various deities, but the old plaster is now crumbling away, making most of the paintings unrecognizable. Inside the sanctum, one can find a north-facing stone image of Akṣobhya.

_source.displaydescription:
The Gãdyaḥ Phalcā is located at Pukhusi, Sunaguthi (widely known as Sunakothi) at the junction where a street leading towards Kulimha curves away from the Sunāguthi main road.

No evidence could so far be traced with which to date the initial construction of this Phalcā. The photo published in Pruscha 1975 (vol. 1), 99 shows the building's original structure before it was rebuilt in 1995 due to damage suffered by its earlier five-bayed structure. The reconstruction saw the addition of a blank masonry wall to the rear and eastern sides. The Phalcā is open to the south and west directions, though it is protected by a grill. Two small metal doors are fixed to the southern wall. The foundation stone of the old structure can be seen on the plinth, and some of the salvaged roof tiles are stacked on top of the roof slab.

The Phalcā has socio-cultural importance for Patan. The masks of the Navadurgās from Thecva are stored here during the Mohanī festival before they are taken to way to (and return from) a performance at Mūla Coka (LAL1260) at Patan Darbar Square. Local residents come here to worship the masks and take part in a procession around Sunaguthi. The procession is followed by a dance performance in front of Kvaylāchī Phalcā (SUN4200).

_source.displaydescription:
Ghana Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, LAL2260), is a small area surrounded by a historic, private building to the north, the Mahākāla Phalcā to the east, the Vajradhara Phalcā to the west and small buildings and a boundary wall to the south. Ghanānanda Śākya, a grandson of Amṛtānanda Vande (the man who taught Buddhism to Brian Hodgson), established this bāhāḥ and it is from him that it gets its name.

The small, single-roofed domed shrine is made of bricks and contains a stone image of Akṣobhya in its sanctum. Akṣobhya is facing west, and there is a rounded dharmadhātu maṇḍala in front of him. The shrine itself is located between the two phalcās and rests on a single plinth. Parts of the base and the dome have been plastered with lime and white-washed, and the walls are built of daci apa and decorative bricks. The stone doorway features an arch with the Five Buddhas carved on it. A well can be found to the south of the shrine.

No historical document could be found to provide the exact date the bāhāḥ was constructed. However, it is possible to estimate a rough date with the help of sources that tell us about Ghanānanda's life more generally. Ghanānanda is mentioned in an inscription dated NS 955 (Śākya 1994, 55-56). Furthermore, in NS 975 (1855 CE), on the first anniversary of his death, a dharmadhātu maṇḍala was established in front of the Mahābuddha Temple (LAL2340) in his honour (Śākya 1988, 88-89) . This suggests that the bāhāḥ was established before 1854 and very probably after 1835.

_source.displaydescription: This Licchavi caitya is located to the north of the street that leads to Karuṇamaya Temple (BUN0001) just after passing the Dey Pukhu. It is built on top of a square base measuring 90 x 90 cm and with total height of 145 cm. Only the upper part of the caitya seems to be from the original Licchavi structure. Stone slabs have been placed aroud the base of the caitya, forming a roof-like form over the square base and the stone statues in its walls. H. Śākya (1993, 72) refers to this monument as Caturdvāreṣu Caityāṅkita Caitya. A few decades ago, a functioning hiti (stone spout) could be found to the east of the Gaṇeśa Mandira (BUN0025) of the Kotā Ṭola. Later, water stopped flowing from the spout and it fell into disuse. Now, the area is full of refuse, and the spout area has been covered with mud. Before it was filled in, a Licchavi period caitya, a statue of Bhagīratha, the original spout and some other statues were moved away from the hiti to their present locations. Bhagīratha’s statue and the spout have been fixed to the new hiti, which is located in front of the Gaṇeśa Mandira.  Bangdel (1995, 358) dates the Bhagīratha statue to the 9th century. A statue of Umāmaheśvara (which is dated by Bangdel (1995, 357) to the 9th century) has been placed on the western side of the present caitya. Its western niche remains empty. According to local residents, there was a statue of Nārāyaṇa in the niche. However, this was stolen around 1994. The northern niche of the caitya has a deteriorated statue which is thought to be Śivapārvatī. A Licchavi caitya has been joined to the upper part of the Caturdvāreṣu Caityāṅkita Caitya. The upper caitya has small caitya-shaped objects in its four niches. The garbha has been damaged in many places, and has been joined to the niche and the harmikās with cement. To the east of this caitya, one can find a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya which was established here in 1956. Local residents worship this caitya whilst visiting other shrines in the morning.
